paragraphs: In the almost peaceful stage of society, the gentleman of leisure consumes more of the necessities of life than he needs to survive and stay healthy. But his consumption also becomes specialised in the quality of the goods. He consumes freely, and he consumes the best: in food, drink, drugs, housing, services, jewellery, clothes, weapons and equipment, entertainment, lucky charms, and even idols or gods. Over time, the things he consumes slowly improve. The main reason for these improvements is no doubt that better and more elaborate products give more personal comfort and well-being. But this does not remain the only purpose. A standard of reputation is also present, and it decides which new things deserve to survive. Consuming these excellent goods is proof of wealth, so it becomes a source of honour. In the same way, failing to consume enough goods of the right quality becomes a sign of inferiority and lack of merit.

This growing attention to small differences in the quality of food, drink and other goods soon affects the gentleman's whole way of life. It also affects his training and his intellectual activity. He is no longer simply the successful, aggressive man of strength, skill and courage. To avoid looking foolish, he must also develop his taste, because he now has to judge carefully between noble and common goods. He becomes an expert in fine food of different qualities, in manly drinks and small ornaments, in suitable clothes and buildings, and in weapons, games, dancers and drugs. Developing this sense of beauty takes time and effort. As a result, the demands on the gentleman tend to change his life of leisure into fairly hard work: he must learn how to live a visible life of leisure in a proper way. Closely connected to the rule that he must consume plenty of the right goods is a second rule. He must know how to consume them in a proper manner. His life of leisure must follow the correct forms. This is the origin of good manners, as an earlier chapter explained. Refined manners and ways of living are simply a way of following the norm of conspicuous leisure and conspicuous consumption, that is, leisure and spending that are meant to be seen.

For the gentleman of leisure, conspicuous consumption of valuable goods is a way to gain a good reputation. But as his wealth grows, his own efforts are no longer enough to display his riches in this way. So he gets help from friends and competitors by giving valuable presents, expensive feasts and entertainments. Presents and feasts probably had another origin than simple showing off. But they became useful for this purpose very early, and they have kept this character until today. In fact, this usefulness has long been the real basis of these customs. Expensive entertainments, such as the potlatch or the ball, are especially suited to this aim. Through them, the host uses the competitor he wants to compare himself with. The guest consumes on behalf of his host. At the same time, he witnesses the large amount of good things that the host cannot consume alone. He also sees how easily the host follows the rules of etiquette.
